Question 1

  1. Write the following function. Give examples to test your function.

  • Input: a data frame

  • Output: a data frame with all the missing of numeric variables replaced by the associated means.

Hint: Similar function

Solution

The loop checks each column. For a numeric column, it replaces NA with the mean of the observed values. Non-numeric columns stay unchanged.

numeric_impute <- function(d) {
  for (i in seq_along(d)) {
    if (is.numeric(d[[i]])) {
      # A completely missing column has no observed mean.
      if (any(!is.na(d[[i]]))) {
        column_mean <- mean(d[[i]], na.rm = TRUE)
        d[[i]][is.na(d[[i]])] <- column_mean
      }
    }
  }
  return(d)
}
missing_data <- data.frame(
  age = c(20, NA, 30, 40, NA, 50),
  spending = c(100, 120, NA, 160, 180, NA),
  group = c("A", NA, "A", "B", "A", NA),
  region = factor(c("North", "North", NA, "South", "North", NA)),
  member = c(TRUE, NA, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, NA)
)

missing_data
##   age spending group region member
## 1  20      100     A  North   TRUE
## 2  NA      120  <NA>  North     NA
## 3  30       NA     A   <NA>   TRUE
## 4  40      160     B  South  FALSE
## 5  NA      180     A  North   TRUE
## 6  50       NA  <NA>   <NA>     NA
numeric_result <- numeric_impute(missing_data)
numeric_result
##   age spending group region member
## 1  20      100     A  North   TRUE
## 2  35      120  <NA>  North     NA
## 3  30      140     A   <NA>   TRUE
## 4  40      160     B  South  FALSE
## 5  35      180     A  North   TRUE
## 6  50      140  <NA>   <NA>     NA
colSums(is.na(numeric_result))
##      age spending    group   region   member 
##        0        0        2        2        2
# The observed age mean is 35, and the observed spending mean is 140.
stopifnot(all(numeric_result$age[c(2, 5)] == 35),
          all(numeric_result$spending[c(3, 6)] == 140),
          identical(numeric_result$group, missing_data$group))

The numeric columns now have no missing values. The categorical and logical columns still have their original missing values, as intended. If a column is entirely missing, its mean cannot be calculated, so those values remain missing.

Question 2

  1. Write the following function. Give examples to test your function.

  • Input: a data frame

  • Output: a data frame with all the missing of variables replaced by the associated means (for numeric variables) or modes (for non-numeric variables).

Hint: Use If-statement to combine the function in Problem 1 and the function in this example

Solution

I use a helper function to find the most frequent observed value, which is the statistical mode. Then an if statement chooses mean imputation for numeric columns and mode imputation for the other columns.

mode_impute <- function(x) {
  observed <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(observed) == 0) return(x)

  counts <- table(observed)
  mode_name <- names(counts)[which.max(counts)]

  # Take the value from the original vector to preserve its type.
  mode_value <- observed[match(mode_name, as.character(observed))]
  x[is.na(x)] <- mode_value
  return(x)
}

all_impute <- function(d) {
  for (i in seq_along(d)) {
    if (is.numeric(d[[i]])) {
      if (any(!is.na(d[[i]]))) {
        d[[i]][is.na(d[[i]])] <- mean(d[[i]], na.rm = TRUE)
      }
    } else {
      d[[i]] <- mode_impute(d[[i]])
    }
  }
  return(d)
}
complete_result <- all_impute(missing_data)
complete_result
##   age spending group region member
## 1  20      100     A  North   TRUE
## 2  35      120     A  North   TRUE
## 3  30      140     A  North   TRUE
## 4  40      160     B  South  FALSE
## 5  35      180     A  North   TRUE
## 6  50      140     A  North   TRUE
colSums(is.na(complete_result))
##      age spending    group   region   member 
##        0        0        0        0        0
stopifnot(!anyNA(complete_result),
          all(complete_result$group[c(2, 6)] == "A"),
          all(as.character(complete_result$region[c(3, 6)]) == "North"),
          all(complete_result$member[c(2, 6)]),
          is.factor(complete_result$region),
          is.logical(complete_result$member))

The modes are A, North, and TRUE. The factor and logical columns keep their types. If categories tie, the first tied category in table() order is used. An entirely missing column stays missing because it has no observed mean or mode. These functions return a new data frame; the original missing_data still contains its missing values.

all_missing <- data.frame(
  number = c(NA_real_, NA_real_),
  category = c(NA_character_, NA_character_)
)
all_impute(all_missing)
##   number category
## 1     NA     <NA>
## 2     NA     <NA>
stopifnot(identical(all_impute(all_missing), all_missing))

Question 3

  1. Write the following function. Give examples to test your function.

  • Input: a data frame

  • Output: Bar plots of all non-numeric variables

Hint: Similar function

Solution

This function loops through the columns and prints a bar plot whenever the column is non-numeric. print() displays each plot inside the loop. It also returns the plots invisibly in a list so I can check their number.

bar_plot <- function(d) {
  plots <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(d)) {
    if (!is.numeric(d[[i]])) {
      p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = .data[[names(d)[i]]])) +
        geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
        labs(title = paste("Counts of", names(d)[i]),
             x = names(d)[i], y = "Count") +
        theme_minimal()
      print(p)
      plots[[names(d)[i]]] <- p
    }
  }
  return(invisible(plots))
}

The following small, made-up dataset is used to test the plotting functions. It has three numeric columns and two categorical columns.

plot_data <- data.frame(
  age = c(20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 32, 35, 37, 40, 42, 45, 47),
  spending = c(120, 100, 150, 180, 160, 210, 230, 200, 240, 260, 250, 290),
  score = c(60, 65, 64, 70, 72, 75, 74, 80, 81, 85, 84, 88),
  group = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), 6)),
  region = rep(c("North", "South", "West"), each = 4)
)
plot_data
##    age spending score group region
## 1   20      120    60     A  North
## 2   22      100    65     B  North
## 3   25      150    64     A  North
## 4   27      180    70     B  North
## 5   30      160    72     A  South
## 6   32      210    75     B  South
## 7   35      230    74     A  South
## 8   37      200    80     B  South
## 9   40      240    81     A   West
## 10  42      260    85     B   West
## 11  45      250    84     A   West
## 12  47      290    88     B   West
single_bars <- bar_plot(plot_data)

length(single_bars)
## [1] 2
stopifnot(length(single_bars) == 2)

There are two plots: one for group and one for region. Each bar counts the rows in that category.

Question 4

  1. Write the following function. Give examples to test your function.

  • Input: a data frame

  • Output: all possible the bar plots of a non-numeric variable filled by a non-numeric variable.

Hint: Similar function

Solution

The two loops consider every pair of columns. The if statement keeps two distinct non-numeric columns. Swapping the x and fill variables gives a different layout, so this version shows both directions.

bar_plot2 <- function(d) {
  plots <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(d)) {
    for (j in seq_along(d)) {
      if (i != j && !is.numeric(d[[i]]) && !is.numeric(d[[j]])) {
        p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = .data[[names(d)[i]]],
                           fill = .data[[names(d)[j]]])) +
          geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
          labs(title = paste(names(d)[i], "filled by", names(d)[j]),
               x = names(d)[i], y = "Count", fill = names(d)[j]) +
          theme_minimal()
        print(p)
        plot_name <- paste(names(d)[i], names(d)[j], sep = "_by_")
        plots[[plot_name]] <- p
      }
    }
  }
  return(invisible(plots))
}
grouped_bars <- bar_plot2(plot_data)

names(grouped_bars)
## [1] "group_by_region" "region_by_group"
length(grouped_bars)
## [1] 2
stopifnot(length(grouped_bars) == 2)

The plots show group filled by region and region filled by group. With two categorical columns there are 2 * (2 - 1) = 2 such plots.

Question 5

  1. Write the following function. Give examples to test your function.

  • Input: a data frame

  • Output:

    • all possible the bar plots of a non-numeric variable filled by a non-numeric variable.

    • all possible the density plots of a numeric variable colored by a non-numeric variable

    • all possible the scatter plots.

Hint: Combine this function, this function, and the function in Question 4. One way to combine is creating a new function, quick_plot, and call these three functions within quick_plot.

Solution

I combine bar_plot2() with a density function and a scatterplot function. The density function checks every numeric/categorical combination, regardless of column order. The scatterplot function uses i < j so each pair of numeric columns is plotted once.

density_plot2 <- function(d) {
  plots <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(d)) {
    for (j in seq_along(d)) {
      if (is.numeric(d[[i]]) && !is.numeric(d[[j]])) {
        p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = .data[[names(d)[i]]],
                           color = .data[[names(d)[j]]])) +
          geom_density(na.rm = TRUE) +
          labs(title = paste(names(d)[i], "by", names(d)[j]),
               x = names(d)[i], y = "Density", color = names(d)[j]) +
          theme_minimal()
        print(p)
        plot_name <- paste(names(d)[i], names(d)[j], sep = "_by_")
        plots[[plot_name]] <- p
      }
    }
  }
  return(invisible(plots))
}

scatter_plot <- function(d) {
  plots <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(d)) {
    for (j in seq_along(d)) {
      if (i < j && is.numeric(d[[i]]) && is.numeric(d[[j]])) {
        p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = .data[[names(d)[i]]],
                           y = .data[[names(d)[j]]])) +
          geom_point(color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
          labs(title = paste(names(d)[i], "and", names(d)[j]),
               x = names(d)[i], y = names(d)[j]) +
          theme_minimal()
        print(p)
        plot_name <- paste(names(d)[i], names(d)[j], sep = "_and_")
        plots[[plot_name]] <- p
      }
    }
  }
  return(invisible(plots))
}

quick_plot <- function(d) {
  bar_plots <- bar_plot2(d)
  density_plots <- density_plot2(d)
  scatter_plots <- scatter_plot(d)
  return(invisible(list(bars = bar_plots, densities = density_plots,
                        scatters = scatter_plots)))
}
all_plots <- quick_plot(plot_data)

c(Bars = length(all_plots$bars),
  Densities = length(all_plots$densities),
  Scatters = length(all_plots$scatters))
##      Bars Densities  Scatters 
##         2         6         3
stopifnot(length(all_plots$bars) == 2,
          length(all_plots$densities) == 6,
          length(all_plots$scatters) == 3)

The combined function prints 11 plots. There are 2 grouped bar plots, 3 * 2 = 6 density plots, and 3 * (3 - 1) / 2 = 3 scatterplots. The density examples have at least four observations per category.

The numeric plots use numeric columns as stored in the input data. A categorical variable coded with numbers should be converted to a factor before calling these functions. The .data[[...]] notation selects a column using its name inside a loop.
